newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone rulers seek all-party conference.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone rulers seek all-party conference.

text.p: Sierra Leone's military rulers called on Tuesday for an all-party consultative conference in which a timetable for fresh elections would be discussed.

Colonel Abdul Sesay, director of military information, told Reuters the conference would bring together the army, Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, the civilian president overthrown on May 25, Revolutionary United Front (RUF) rebels and the Kamajor civil militia.

"We are calling for all the major stake holders in the present political crisis... to sit together and consult in the African tradition and resolve the present political crisis in the country and set a timetable for fresh elections in Sierra Leone in which everybody including Kabbah himself can participate," he said.

The call followed a weekend visit to Freetown by Ghana's deputy foreign minister, James Victor Gbeho, who urged implementation of an Organisation of African Unity call for restoration of constitutional order in Sierra Leone.
"We believe that the best way to resolve the crisis is by diplomatic means, to reach a negotiated settlement, rather than by fighting," Gbeho said.

Sesay said the military rulers of Sierra Leone, who forged an alliance with the rebels after the May 25 coup, wanted "moral guarantors" to attend the talks and the United Nations to provide security at the venue.

He said countries and organisations involved in the peace deal that Kabbah signed in November with RUF leader Foday Sankoh in Ivory Coast could be "moral guarantors" along with former colonial power Britain and the United States.
Sesay said the timing of the conference would depend on logistical arrangements and discussions between the parties.

Other agenda items would be demobilisation and reintegration of rebel fighters, addressing the grievances of the military and ensuring the welfare of all involved in the coup, consolidation of the peace deal with the rebels and reaching consensus on what constitutes goods governance for a civilian government.

Kabbah, who took office in March 1996 after multi-party elections ended four years of army rule, used the Kamajor traditional hunters as a civil militia to help the army push back the rebels who took up arms in 1991. He is currently in neighbouring Guinea.

Civilian politicians and Sierra Leone's West African neighbours insist that Kabbah be reinstated, something the coup leaders have rejected. Kamajor leaders rejected an offer from the coup leaders to join a broad-based government, saying they want to stay out of politics.
Nigerian gunboats bombarded the capital Freetown in a show of force on June 2 and dissident soldiers and rebels attacked Nigerian soldiers who were there under a defence accord.
A widely anticipated Nigerian attack to restore Kabbah has not materialised.
